content: Kawasaki disease is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries. This condition can result in damage to the coronary arteries, which supply blood to the heart. Early diagnosis is critical because it allows for timely treatment, which can potentially prevent these serious cardiac complications. Salicylate, also known as acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) or aspirin, is commonly used alongside intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) to treat Kawasaki disease. However, the use of salicylate in children is generally avoided due to concerns about severe side effects, particularly the risk of Reye's syndrome. The purpose of this review was to assess the effectiveness of salicylate in treating Kawasaki disease and preventing its associated cardiac complications in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted. The Cochrane Peripheral Vascular Diseases Group searched their trials register and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) up to January 2009. Additionally, databases such as MEDLINE (from January 1966 to July 2006), EMBASE (from January 1980 to July 2006), and CINAHL (from 1982 to July 2006) were searched. Reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed, and experts in the field were contacted for further information. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the use of salicylate in treating Kawasaki disease in children. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. Study authors were contacted to obtain additional details when necessary. The review identified one trial involving 102 children, which was described as randomized. However, the method of treatment allocation could not be confirmed. A second comparative study, which may have used randomization for treatment allocation, was also identified. In the first trial, the addition of ASA to IVIG treatment did not show a significant effect on the rate of coronary artery abnormalities at follow-up, although the confidence intervals were wide. The second study, which compared high-dose ASA to low-dose ASA, demonstrated a reduction in the duration of fever with high-dose ASA. However, this study lacked sufficient power to determine the effect of ASA on coronary artery abnormalities at follow-up. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence to determine whether salicylate should be included in the treatment regimen for children with Kawasaki disease. High-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to clarify the role of salicylate in this context.
